cite_runs: [Justin Kollar, Department of Architecture, College of Design and Engineering @ National University of Singapore, “GOVERNING THE CLOUD: Infrastructural Statecraft and the Political Ecology of Digital Expansion in Oregon” SATS: Northern European Journal of Philosophy, 20 April 2026, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1468-2427.70098] aa 🪼
body: Examining Amazon, Google, and Intel, the article traces how fiscal incentives, utility programs, and land-use instruments are recalibrated to secure hyperscale loads. Through a political-ecological lens, it shows governance shifting from public deliberation to contractual and executive venues, including PPAs, special-service tariffs, confidentiality agreements, and expedited siting, facilitating rapid buildout while externalizing socio-ecological costs to municipalities and ecosystems. Case studies in The Dalles, Morrow/Umatilla, and Hillsboro demonstrate how ‘systems-integration’ by state and utility actors couples energy, water, and land as a single infrastructure, narrows transparency and contestation, and locks local institutions into long-duration commitments.

The article advances urban political ecology and infrastructure studies by theorizing a digital metabolic regime and by specifying infrastructural dependency as an engineered modality of power. The study concludes that governing digital expansion requires reintegrating energy–water–land assessment, restoring disclosure and public standing in decision venues, and tying incentives to verifiable performance and community benefit. Beneath the veneer of frictionless digital exchange, the global cloud is grounded in vast and uneven material infrastructures.

The dematerialized, placeless infrastructure of the cloud is, in fact, a project of territorial extraction and political transformation. Cloud capital—the fusion of platform-based accumulation with the infrastructural and material demands of digital systems—reshapes urban-regional landscapes through a new alignment of corporate, state, and financial power. Understanding these shifts requires an analytic frame that links digital infrastructures to wider political, economic, and ecological transformations. Oregon's recent experience offers a concentrated view of a broader global pattern of uneven development and extraction.

oupled with state and local shifts, these moves entrench corporate access to energy, land, and water while weakening mechanisms for public oversight and deliberation. The foundations for these policies were laid well before 2025. In the late 2010s and early 2020s, surging demand for energy-intensive AI compute and cloud services, coupled with the CHIPS Acts, positioned semiconductor fabrication and digital infrastructure as pillars of US industrial policy. Oregon, once oriented to agriculture, timber, and post–Cold War deindustrialization, pivoted toward high tech as state and local governments increasingly acted as systems integrators for cloud and chip expansion.

Programs designed for high-wage manufacturing thus came to underwrite capital-intensive, labor-sparse infrastructure, leaving communities with durable utility and fiscal obligations for uncertain long-run gains. These shifts reveal a deeper transformation under cloud capitalism. Rather than merely regulating industry, the state increasingly acts as a ‘systems integrator’, coupling energy, water, and land as contractual assets and engineering path-dependent infrastructural dependencies that privatize control and returns while socializing risk and ecological harm. These dynamics materialize differently across the cloud supply chain, which clarifies their territorial effects. Semiconductor fabrication plants (fabs) and hyperscale data centers both consume water and electricity at the scale of small cities, yet fabs anchor supplier ecosystems and sizable employment, while data centers create few jobs and convert local utilities into dedicated service providers for a handful of private loads. Meeting these always-on baselines bundles grid upgrades, water entitlements, and land conversions into a single planning problem, provoking backlash over rate hikes, water stress, and infrastructure crowd-out. Recent contests—ranging from zoning defeats that halted a multibillion-dollar project in Peculiar, Missouri, to a voter recall that stopped a major proposal in Cascade Locks, Oregon—signal the rising salience of these costs. At the same time, the decisive arena is shifting upward: because authority over electricity, siting, and water is state-mediated, legislatures are fast-tracking interconnections and pre-empting local control, extending the state-utility systems-integrator model even where municipal consent is contested. A restructuring of infrastructural governance embeds extractive spatial logics within public planning. Marketed as immaterial or ‘green’, cloud infrastructures depend on expansive energy, land, and water hinterlands, disproportionately impacting rural and peri-urban territories (Diguet and Lopez, 2019; Farmer, 2023; Monstadt and Saltzman, 2025). Data centers and fabs now compete with communities for scarce water, land, and power, often advancing under loosened oversight and minimal public input. These entanglements raise fundamental questions that drive this study: who governs critical infrastructural flows under cloud capitalism, and how are public institutions repurposed to serve private accumulation strategies? The Oregon case shows how the expansion of cloud capital restructures territorial governance, erodes democratic accountability, and embeds corporate control within the everyday management of energy, water, and land systems. This article contributes to discourse in urban political ecology (UPE) and infrastructure studies in three linked ways. First, extending UPE's metabolic lens (Heynen et al., 2006; Swyngedouw, 2006), it specifies a digital metabolic regime in which data centers and fabs reconfigure coupled energy–water–land flows, shifting socio-ecological costs to rural and peri-urban territories while ‘green’ narratives obscure these transfers. Second, building on work on opacity and exception in digital infrastructures (Amoore, 2018; Bridges, 2024; Brodie et al., 2024), it shows how governance shifts in practice from public forums to contractual and executive venues—PPAs, confidentiality agreements, utility dockets, and gubernatorial instruments—where transparency and contestation are constrained. Thus, to paraphrase Amoore (2018: 9), the aim of ‘wrest[ing] the cloud into an intelligible form’ is a central political task to achieve accountability and oversight. Third, it foregrounds infrastructural dependency as a modality of power. Once budgets, grids, and water systems are tuned to hyperscale loads, exit costs steepen, and political choice narrows, underscoring the need to repoliticize planning and regulation to address the digital economy's socio-ecological footprint. The analysis proceeds through three interrelated empirical sites that map the architecture of this regime. In The Dalles, Google's data centers have reweighted the municipal budget and hydro-infrastructural regime while pushing key usage data behind claims of confidentiality. In Morrow and Umatilla Counties, Amazon's expansion has intensified emissions and grid dependencies, with a rural cooperative purchasing fossil-heavy power to meet surging loads even as new renewable projects are announced. In Hillsboro, Intel's manufacturing drive has catalyzed statutory mechanisms to override land-use protections and expand urban growth boundaries in the name of industrial competitiveness. Across these cases, cloud capital consolidates its territorial footprint through tax policy, regulatory exception, and infrastructural investment—under the aegis of national security, innovation, and ‘green’ modernization. Methodology and theoretical framing This study adopts a conjunctural approach to make sense of the current transformational moment in the political economy of infrastructure in Oregon (and globally). By conjuncture, I mean the alignment of elements that usually move on different timescales—federal industrial strategy and permitting reforms, state land-use and utility instruments, investment and market cycles, and firm siting decisions—whose entanglement is reorganizing energy, water, and land. In this spirit, conjunctural analysis is ‘focused on the analysis of politically salient situations, places, and moments’, working to ‘disentangle intersecting and articulated sources of conditioning and causality’ while remaining ‘explicitly situated in space and time’ (Peck, 2023: 462). Thus, rather than treating The Dalles, Umatilla–Morrow, and Hillsboro as discrete cases, I read them as co-constituted sites within a single articulable situation, each illustrating how similar strategies meet hyperscale demand under different local conditions but operationalized within a regional and planetary system. The methods and sources reflect this conjunctural approach. I analyze public records and budgets, utility and commission filings, legislative testimony and statutes, company documents, local and national reporting, and site-specific studies. Using fiscal records, regulatory filings, and investigative reporting collected between 2023 and 2025, I map how governance over infrastructure and land use is being restructured across financial, legal, and resource systems. Because the conjuncture is multi-sited and multiscalar, documents from municipal councils, cooperatives and investor-owned utilities, state agencies, regional power markets, and federal programs are read together rather than in isolation. Although qualitative, the approach emphasizes reproducibility by privileging publicly verifiable sources, while acknowledging that data availability and granularity vary by state. Viewed conjuncturally, Oregon's expansion of data centers and semiconductor facilities provides a sharp vantage on broader shifts in capitalism's spatial organization, infrastructural governance, and state power. Digital capitalism does not transcend place—it takes form through energy-, land-, and water-intensive systems rooted in specific regions. These material demands expose the institutional arrangements that sustain the ‘cloud’, a formation I call here cloud capital: the fusion of platform accumulation with the physical infrastructures and regulatory alignments that make it possible. Far from immaterial, the cloud depends on vast networks of electricity, cooling water, land siting, and transmission corridors (Burrington, 2014; Hu, 2016; Hogan and Vonderau, 2019; Narayan, 2022). Recent scholarship traces these material underpinnings, showing how data-center development relies on localized ‘spatial fixes’—stable utility supply, permissive regulation, and favorable fiscal regimes—to secure capital investment (Diguet and Lopez, 2019; Furlong, 2021; Brodie et al., 2024; Edwards et al., 2024). From urban colocation hubs to rural hyperscale campuses, data centers now reconfigure land-use systems and embed themselves within power plants, substations, fiber routes, and water networks, extending resource hinterlands deep into rural regions and the global South (Ristic et al., 2015; Al Kez et al., 2022; Monstadt and Saltzman, 2025). Building on urban metabolism in UPE (Heynen et al., 2006; Swyngedouw, 2006), I conceptualize a digital metabolic regime through three interrelated mechanisms. The first concerns how cloud infrastructure reconfigures energy, water, and land as coupled rather than separate systems. Hyperscale, always-on operations integrate electricity supply, cooling water, and land siting into a single planning problem: new interconnections require new cooling and effluent routes; water entitlements demand pumping power and thermal rejection; land conversions necessitate transmission capacity and heat management. This coupling recasts peri-urban and rural areas as low-capacity yet highly exploitable hinterlands—intensive zones of computation serving urban cores. Extending UPE's metabolic lens to digital infrastructures also reveals how ‘green’ or carbon-neutral efficiency narratives obscure and displace socio-ecological costs across territories (Hogan, 2015; 2018; Tan, 2019). These transformations are not just technical but are politically secured through incentives, preferential tariffs, and public-private arrangements that align multi-agency governance around hyperscale demands. The second mechanism involves a rescaling of governance from jurisdictional forums to contractual and executive instruments. While statutes, hearings, and public votes persist in form, the binding decisions increasingly reside in power purchase agreements, confidentiality clauses, special-service contracts, utility dockets, and executive authorities enabled by statute. These venues narrow transparency, public standing, and opportunities for contestation (Amoore, 2018; Bridges, 2024; Brodie et al., 2024). Siting projects in suburban business parks or repurposed industrial zones—shielded by ‘trade secret’ claims and fragmented oversight—further insulates them from comprehensive review and obscures cumulative, cross-sector impacts (Holt and Vonderau, 2017; Pickren, 2018; Diguet and Lopez, 2019; Brodie, 2020; Libertson et al., 2021; Farmer, 2023). Through such contracts, local decisions become bound to translocal corporate and developer agreements, shifting leverage beyond any single jurisdiction. In effect, the coupled resource flows identified earlier are now governed through instruments that increasingly make traditional planning and regulatory frameworks ill-suited to the scale and interdependence of cloud infrastructure. The third mechanism frames infrastructural dependency as a modality of power, produced by load profiles, resource coupling, and financialization. Classic accounts place infrastructure at the core of state power (Ferguson, 1990; Graham and Marvin, 2001; Mitchell, 2002; Larkin, 2013). Here, dependency is not incidental but engineered. Hyperscale's baseloads shift utilities from managing peaks to delivering persistent, contract-anchored service at the scale of a small city. Because energy, water, and land are coupled, a commitment in one domain cascades into binding obligations in the others. These linkages create systemic dependencies that expand with market growth and expose utilities and municipalities to volatility when demand or resource conditions change. Financialization then converts offtake contracts, tax credits, and renewable procurements into asset-class returns—via tax-advantaged projects, private equity vehicles, and public pension capital (O'Neill, 2019; Braun and Christophers, 2024; Christophers, 2024). This results in rising exit costs for local authorities, the migration of revenue and control rights to distant balance sheets, and a narrowed policy space precisely as local obligations deepen. Taken together, these mechanisms explain how cloud capital restructures socio-ecological systems and state power—by rerouting resource flows, shifting authority upward and outward, and locking public institutions into private accumulation. This framework extends UPE and infrastructure studies by making metabolism explicitly digital and coupled, and by casting opacity and exception as contractual modes of rule. It also reframes classic state–infrastructure accounts around engineered dependencies produced by always-on loads and land–water–energy coupling. Most pointedly, it demonstrates how public institutions become structurally committed to reproducing private digital infrastructures as decision-making shifts toward contractual and financial centers that are difficult to contest. Situating the ‘Silicon Forest’ Once a regional label for high tech west of Portland, the ‘Silicon Forest’ now describes a statewide landscape of data centers and semiconductor fabs reshaping Oregon's economy, institutions, and resource systems. Early anchors like Tektronix and Intel have been joined by hyperscale cloud campuses and AI hubs, making Oregon a testing ground for how global firms use fiscal incentives, utility restructuring, and state intervention to secure land, power, and water. While chip manufacturing remains a major employer, the current wave is led by data centers that create few jobs yet exert outsized pressure on grids, water supplies, and rural land. Three sites illustrate this dynamic across rural, peri-urban, and metropolitan contexts—Google in The Dalles, Amazon in Morrow and Umatilla Counties, and Intel in Hillsboro—showing how territorial governance is being reconfigured to serve cloud capital and chip production, and raising questions of accountability, environmental justice, and long-term resilience. Google in The Dalles The high-tech electronics industry highlights a structural power asymmetry, as seasoned corporate counsel and site-selection teams from big tech negotiate with small-town managers, volunteer councilors, and utility engineers while higher levels of government shape the terms of engagement. In Oregon, Enterprise Zones (1985) and the Strategic Investment Program (1993) were originally designed as broad development and job creation tools that function as firm-specific contracts that trade normal taxation for negotiated fees and legal terms such as venue selection, damage caps, and disclaimers on foregone revenue. This shift moves fiscal politics out of public forums and into executive agreements, giving corporations greater influence. Local governments, often strapped for funds and competing for investment, have built administrative systems—assessor-based cash flows, enterprise-zone managers, and intergovernmental resolutions—that make these deals easy to replicate but difficult to challenge. Since the 2010s, Enterprise Zones have mainly benefited data centers owned by Google, Amazon, Facebook, and Apple rather than semiconductor plants (Rogoway, 2022b). While the Strategic Investment Program (SIP) has supported large semiconductor and renewable-energy projects, data centers remain highly automated and generate few jobs compared to the billions spent on computational power, with eight Hillsboro facilities receiving USD 16 million in abatements for only 116 jobs in 2022 (Rogoway, 2023b). Bond-contribution clauses and similar ‘hold harmless’ measures help quiet criticism by offsetting school and service revenues, yet they also lock local budgets and infrastructure planning for energy and water to a single firm's footprint for more than a decade. These arrangements attract and manage capital through opaque, replicable contracts that reshape rural landscapes and utilities around data-center demand despite minimal employment benefits. The Columbia River Basin has emerged as a prime location for data centers due to its cheap electricity, abundant rural land, and access to high-bandwidth fiber optics. Supporting over 40% of US hydropower, the region attracts major tech companies like Google and Amazon (Lillis, 2014). State tax incentives on intangible assets have further spurred development. Hillsboro, a city near Portland, illustrates this growth with its cluster of data centers and role as a terminus for major trans-Pacific submarine cables (see Figure 1). While these infrastructures strengthen global digital networks and support urban tech hubs like Portland, their benefits often bypass the local communities that host them. Data centers predominantly serve distant markets, perpetuating a pattern of resource extraction from rural areas with minimal returns for local residents, despite promises of fostering local economic development (Mahmoudi et al., 2020). Details are in the caption following the image FIGURE 1 Open in figure viewer PowerPoint Oregon network and geographic context (map by author using data from Infrapedia, Datacenters.com) The Dalles, Oregon, offers a revealing case of how local governments reorient themselves to attract and sustain corporate infrastructure. After Lockheed Martin's aluminum smelter closed, the city sought economic revival through a tax deal with Google, resulting in the company's first data center in 2006. That project soon became a model for similar developments statewide. Concerns emerged, however, about relying on a single employer, echoing the economic disruption caused by Lockheed's exit (Rogoway, 2015). Over the years, Google has secured hundreds of millions in tax breaks while employing only about 200 people. In 2021, the company proposed a major expansion, including two additional data centers, in exchange for another 15-year tax abatement through Oregon's SIP. City officials approved the plan and negotiated a water access deal in which Google would donate 35 acres and fund infrastructure upgrades in return for exclusive access to a confidential volume of water. The agreement also included plans to develop groundwater rights and re-inject treated water into the aquifer, a move expected to triple the city's supply—though whether the benefits primarily serve residents or Google remains unclear. Although The Dalles sits along the Columbia River, it faces drought risks that have raised alarms among farmers, environmentalists, and Yakama Nation tribal fishers. The nearby Dog River, home to three endangered fish species, could be affected by increased industrial water use. Disputes over Google's secretive water data escalated when The Oregonian/OregonLive filed a public records request. Google and the city, citing a confidentiality agreement, refused, prompting a lawsuit that Google helped fund. After a 13-month legal battle, they agreed to release the data and paid USD 53,000 to the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press. Records showed Google's water use tripled between 2017 and 2021, reaching 355 million gallons (1.34 million cubic meters)—or 29% of the city's total. Despite scrutiny, The Dalles approved the tax breaks in 2022 and, in 2024, finalized plans for Google's AI data center expansion and infrastructure investments. Google's establishment of its first data center in The Dalles significantly impacted the Northwest Wasco County People's Utility District (NWCPUD), becoming its largest customer. Though NWCPUD's reports do not name the company directly, in 2005 it listed five unidentified ‘primary service customers’, increasing to six after Google's arrival in 2006, indicating a substantial contribution to utility revenues. Between 2005 and 2009, sales from these customers rose from USD 1.4 million to USD 13.8 million, with one report estimating Google's annual energy costs at USD 12.4 million for roughly 330 gigawatt-hours in 2009 (Oregon Business Team, 2010). By 2015, the top five customers consumed 417 gigawatt-hours, making up 69 percent of sales and generating USD 17.5 million in gross revenue, likely driven by Google (NWCPUD, 2016). This dependency was underscored in a report noting that if Google shut down in FY2018, NWCPUD would lose USD 3.7 million in net revenues, potentially requiring an 18% rate hike for other customers. To fund the major infrastructure upgrades required for Google, NWCPUD raised rates. From 2016 to 2021, residential electricity prices rose from USD 68.00 to USD 77.71 per megawatt-hour, while usage increased modestly from 129.3 to 133.0 gigawatt-hours. Residential revenues grew from USD 8.8 million (27.2% of total revenue) to USD 10.3 million (17.3%), largely tracking inflation. In contrast, commercial and industrial revenues, with Google as the main customer, nearly doubled from USD 21.6 million (66.8%) to USD 48.3 million (80.8%) over the same period. Although exact usage under Google's special contract remains undisclosed, the company's expansion to five data centers and USD 1.8 billion in investment in The Dalles clearly drove this growth. By 2023, commercial and industrial revenues had surged to USD 80.9 million (84.2%), while residential revenues were USD 11.0 million (11.4%), despite a slight rate drop.2 Figure 2 illustrates these shifts in revenue and the net increase in utility plant assets due to substation and transmission upgrades. Details are in the caption following the image FIGURE 2 Open in figure viewer PowerPoint Northern Wasco County People's Utility District sales and fixed capital, 2004 to 2022 (source: Oregon Public Utility Commission) NWCPUD generates around 100 gigawatt-hours annually from its two hydro plants, but most of its energy comes from imported power through contracts and PPAs, primarily to meet Google's massive demand. From 2015 to 2024, energy imports rose in tandem with Google's growth. The utility contracted with another provider under the Western Systems Power Pool from 2015 to 2017 for USD 13.3 million, renewing from 2017 to 2020 for USD 25.1 million. Additional PPAs from 2020 to 2024 totaled USD 50.3 million, averaging USD 10 million annually, much of it directed to ‘one customer’ (likely Google), including large imports from Avangrid Renewables (NWCPUD, 2020: 42). While some power is renewable, natural gas likely filled the supply gap. In 2015, NWCPUD's power mix was 85.3% hydro (525 gigawatt-hours) via the Federal Columbia River Power System. By 2023, hydropower had dropped to 46.5% of total resources, while 47.4% came from ‘unspecified’ regional sources, likely including gas (Ramadan et al., 2024). The Dalles is not the only location in the Columbia River basin facing development pressure for data centers. Amazon and others have built extensively, driving major water and energy upgrades that reshape the regional landscape. These changes have also affected Indigenous lands, including those of the Yakama Nation, where the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission faces a legal dispute over renewable energy infrastructure near culturally sensitive areas (Oaster, 2024). Many projects have been proposed within the Yakama's ceded territory—some opposed, others supported—reflecting the tension between development and tribal sovereignty. The demand for renewable power is partly driven by data center growth, such as Amazon's large-scale expansion upstream, which requires significant new energy generation. Over the past decade, Amazon spent tens of billions expanding data centers in Morrow and Umatilla Counties, leveraging tax breaks worth about USD 50 million annually after deals with local officials, reaching USD 76 million in 2022. In 2023, the Port of Morrow unanimously approved a USD 1 billion incentive package for five new data centers valued at USD 12 billion. Despite modest direct economic returns, some officials involved in these deals found ways to benefit. Shortly after Amazon arrived in Morrow County, local officials who had helped negotiate the deals purchased Inland Development Corp, a nonprofit originally established by the county to deliver fiber capacity for government and healthcare (Rogoway, 2022a). In 2011, it expanded to serve private firms through its subsidiary, Windwave Communications, allowing it to retain nonprofit status. As Amazon scaled up, Windwave's profits tripled between 2013 and 2017. In 2016, Windwave was sold to people already on the nonprofit and Windwave boards, including a county commissioner and the port's former director—all of whom had helped facilitate Amazon's expansion before the sale. Windwave's finances ceased being public after the sale, so total profits remain unclear. The buyers negotiated their acquisition while new tax breaks for Amazon were being considered, raising questions about self-dealing. Between 2016 and 2020, Amazon secured five Enterprise Zone tax deals in Morrow County, saving the company hundreds of millions through property tax exemptions for major investments. These actions sparked scrutiny over whether the officials involved had arranged the terms to their own benefit. Following an investigation, the Oregon Government Ethics Commission fined three former public officials USD 2,000 each in 2024 for ethics violations related to these transactions (Rogoway, 2024c). Amazon in Umatilla and Morrow Counties. The expansion of data centers has led to a sharp rise in carbon emissions. Umatilla Electric Cooperative, which serves Umatilla and Morrow Counties, is now the third-largest emitter of greenhouse gases among Oregon utilities—largely due to one customer: Amazon (Rogoway, 2024a). Despite having only 16,183 customers, the co-op's emissions jumped from 10.6 thousand tons in 2011, when Amazon opened its first Oregon data center, to 1.8 million tons in 2022 (Figure 3). Hydropower from the Bonneville Power Administration (BPA) is already allocated to existing users, forcing Umatilla Electric to purchase additional electricity on the open market, much of it generated by fossil fuels, including a nearby natural gas plant. In 2023 Portland General Electric (PGE) and other power agencies raised their forecasts for data center electricity demand, driven by the rise of AI compute. BPA projects that by 2041 power use by data centers in Oregon and Washington will more than double—equivalent to the consumption of a third of all homes in the two states (Rogoway, 2023c). Details are in the caption following the image FIGURE 3 Open in figure viewer PowerPoint Carbon emissions and emissions/energy ratio for Umatilla Electric Cooperative, 2010 to 2023 (source: Oregon Department of Environmental Quality) In early 2023, state lawmakers introduced a bill to curb emissions by phasing in renewable energy requirements for data centers and cryptocurrency miners by 2040. Amazon opposed the bill, spending over USD 93,000 on lobbying in the first quarter alone. The company argued that the bill imposed mandates without providing incentives to connect renewable projects to the grid and pushed for faster permitting. The bill failed in committee in mid-2023. Instead, legislators extended Enterprise Zone tax incentives, added new semiconductor subsidies, and moved the program's sunset date from 2025 to 2032. Yet, transparency remains a significant issue, as local officials prefer to keep negotiations confidential to protect the company's proprietary information. Public scrutiny over emissions and corporate sustainability pledges has spurred interest in renewable energy buildout, with many new projects directly tied to data-center expansion. Renewable facilities benefit from SIP incentives if the investment is large enough, and most SIP-subsidized projects in the Columbia River Watershed now include wind or solar infrastructure (see Figure 4). Renewables can come online faster than fossil fuel plants but still face resistance due to the need for new transmission lines. Environmentalists, farmers, and property owners have voiced concerns about ecological and land-use impacts, leading to contentious debates over routing and permitting (Williams, 2023). Details are in the caption following the image FIGURE 4 Open in figure viewer PowerPoint Footprint of existing and proposed green energy facilities compared to the Portland area and nearby tribal areas (map by author using data from datacenters.com, USGS, State of Washington, State of Oregon) In addition to generous tax incentives given by local governments, private capital plays a major role in financing renewables tied to cloud infrastructure growth. As discussed previously, this is a core feature of cloud capital. For example, Generate Capital, an infrastructure investment firm focused on renewables, finances projects developed and operated by providers like Pine Gate Renewables. Pine Gate installs solar projects as both turnkey provider and owner-operator and arranges power purchase agreements (PPAs) with companies like Meta. One such project in Temple, Texas supplies Meta's hyperscale data center. Pine Gate now operates more than 100 solar facilities with over two gigawatts of capacity and has over 30 gigawatts in development. These financial networks are closely tied to federal policy. Generate's cofounder, Jigar Shah, led the Department of Energy's Loan Programs Office (LPO) under the Biden administration, directing billions toward renewable infrastructure and de-risking private investment. Meanwhile, public pension funds like California State Teachers’ Retirement System and Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan have invested heavily in renewable projects linked to cloud expansion, including Pine Gate. Together, these actors illustrate how public finance, private equity, and tech-driven energy demand are now deeply entangled through a mix of tax policy, federal lending, and infrastructure capital flows. Amazon has entered into an agreement with Umatilla Electric Cooperative that allows the company to select its own energy supply for its data centers—an arrangement it describes as an ‘innovative solution’. As part of this setup, Pine Gate Renewables is investing in the Sunstone Solar Project (formerly Echo Solar), a proposed 1,200-megawatt solar facility on farmland in eastern Oregon. The project is designed to meet Amazon's renewable energy demands and is the primary reason for Pine Gate's presence in the region.3 In addition to solar, Amazon has contracted wind energy from Avangrid, a subsidiary of the Spanish multinational Iberdrola. As of May 2024, Avangrid's largest customers are data centers, with over seven terawatt-hours contracted that year by firms including Meta, Apple, Microsoft, Google, and Amazon (Iberdrola, 2024: 22). Avangrid also operates the Leaning Juniper IIA wind farm in nearby Gilliam County, a SIP-supported project that claims to generate enough electricity to power 22,800 homes annually—though the energy is primarily used for Amazon's cloud operations.

To address the gap in demand, Amazon has proposed using oxidizing fuel cell technology at three of its Oregon data centers. Although promoted as ‘innovative’, these systems rely on natural gas, sourced via the Gas Transmission Northwest pipeline, to generate power—reducing dependence on hydropower while introducing new carbon emissions. According to the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality, these fuel cells could become the main energy source for the facilities, generating up to 250,000 tons of GHG emissions annually (Rogoway, 2023a). This setup also allows Amazon to bypass regional grid constraints, giving it more direct control over energy sourcing while reducing transparency and public oversight. The rapid buildout of renewable energy projects has become central to cloud capital's legitimacy, linking digital infrastructure growth with socialized finance, including investments from public pension funds. Success depends not just on economic power but on the ability of firms to coordinate legal, political, technical, and real estate expertise to shape outcomes in their favor. However, this dominance raises concerns over environmental injustice and equity. Renewable projects and data center expansions increasingly compete with local communities for land, water, and energy access, often sidelining public interests (Mulvaney, 2024). To bolster its image, AWS has promoted community initiatives such as recycling data center water for agricultural use in Umatilla County (Bellos, 2022). Still, questions persist about whether such efforts are adequate or whether redirected tax revenues and stronger public oversight would offer more equitable benefits. Additionally, data centers generate few long-term jobs, which undercuts the original goal of Oregon's tax incentive programs to attract high-value employment in sectors like semiconductor manufacturing. As I now turn to the state's evolving strategies, it remains unclear whether the current model of cloud expansion will deliver the broader economic development once promised. Intel in Hillsboro. In the Pacific Northwest, attention has been paid to Intel as it pushes into the AI and high-performance-computing market, with Microsoft and Amazon expanding rapidly nearby. Intel is also Oregon's largest private employer, with nearly 23,000 workers at its Washington County campus. In 2021, it invested USD 3 billion to upgrade its Ronler Acres research site in Hillsboro and partnered with PGE on a utility-scale solar project in Wasco County, developed by Avangrid under a PPA through PGE's Green Future Impact program. The following year, Intel announced multibillion-dollar investments in Ohio, Germany, and Ireland in hopes of securing government support abroad. Oregon leaders grew anxious as the state had yet to land comparable semiconductor projects while the CHIPS Act was being drafted. Though Intel proposed a USD 700 million research lab in 2022 to develop more efficient data center cooling near its Hillsboro campus, the project was canceled in 2023 after disappointing sales, heightening concerns that Oregon was falling behind. In February 2022, shortly after Intel announced a USD 20+ billion investment in Ohio (Fedor, 2023),4 the Oregon Semiconductor Competitiveness Task Force was established to safeguard the state's chip industry. Chaired by the Governor, a US Senator, and PGE's CEO, the task force worked with the legislature's Joint Committee on Semiconductors to address incentives, land, and utility needs. Despite Intel receiving hundreds of millions in SIP abatements, including USD 280 million in FY2023,5 the region's lack of large industrial parcels was seen as the main obstacle. Oregon's urban growth boundary (UGB), designed to protect farmland, restricted development of the contiguous land required for new fabs. By contrast, states like Ohio, New York, and Arizona, which were attracting major investments, had ample space for semiconductor ecosystems. Committee testimony underscored these requirements. A single fab could demand 100–300 megawatts of energy and 10–40 million gallons (40–150 thousand cubic meters) of water per day, while suppliers might need 1–10 million gallons (4–40 thousand cubic meters). Doug Smith, International Business Development Manager of the Port of Portland, testified that ‘[t]he success of these companies is not just about a parcel of land of a sufficient size. There have to be sufficient quantities of readily available, even redundant sources, of both public and private utilities’. An industrial land survey recommended two sites of 500 contiguous acres (~200 hectares) each, four sites of 50–100 acres (20–40 hectares) for suppliers, and eight sites of 15–35 acres (6–14 hectares) for key material providers. Potential 500-acre tracts were identified in North Plains and North Hillsboro, with the survey advising expansion into rural reserves to secure suitable land.6 Opposition emerged, particularly from farmers in the Tualatin Valley Irrigation District, who warned that semiconductor development could undermine their irrigation system. The federally built project, with 120 miles of piped infrastructure, sustains crops such as strawberries, green beans, sweet corn, and sugar beet seed. Commenters cautioned that losing farmland would shift the costs of maintaining irrigation onto fewer farmers, threatening long-term viability. Still, these local concerns were overshadowed by arguments about national security. Chris Miller, author of Chip War, highlighted US dependence on Taiwan for advanced semiconductors and the strategic imperatives driving CHIPS Act investments. Legislators also scrutinized Taiwan's industrial strategy, noting the importance of government backing, expedited permitting, and tax incentives in establishing global semiconductor leadership. These deliberations took aim at Oregon's longstanding land use framework. The state's first land use bill, SB 100 of 1973, sought to prevent urban sprawl by establishing UGBs around each city and creating a controlled process for expansion. SB 100 required local governments to prepare comprehensive plans aligned with statewide goals and created the Land Conservation and Development Commission (LCDC) to enforce compliance, emphasizing preservation of farmland, forests, and open space. In 1979, the regional government Metro was established to manage the UGB in the Portland metro area, which includes Washington County. Metro must review UGBs every five years to ensure a 20-year supply of developable land. In 2007, SB 1011 created ‘urban reserves’ and ‘rural reserves’ for the Portland area, identifying land for growth over 40–50 years and protecting farmland from development for 20–30 years beyond standard projections. From 2008 to 2009, Metro's counties engaged citizens and governments to identify suitable areas for these reserves. In Washington County, urban interests dominated,7 resulting in high-value non-irrigated farmland being designated as urban reserves, while irrigated farmland was preserved as rural reserves, despite objections from farmers. From 2009 to 2014, significant high-value non-irrigated farmlands, including hundreds of acres in Helvetia and 1,700 acres in Northwest Hillsboro, were designated as urban reserves. Advocacy groups such as Save Helvetia, 1000 Friends of Oregon, and the Oregon Department of Agriculture argued the county misapplied SB 1011's criteria, relying on a discredited survey. Metro and LCDC nonetheless approved the designations in 2011. The groups appealed, and in 2014, the Oregon Court of Appeals ruled the analysis legally flawed, requiring reversal and remand. The court emphasized that non-irrigated farmland must be treated as equally productive under SB 1011. While other Metro counties complied, Washington County and Hillsboro continued to pursue urban reserve expansion. After the ruling, developers lobbied for legislative intervention. HB 4078, passed in 2014 as the ‘Grand Bargain’, ratified much of Metro's 2011 plan. It approved South Hillsboro development, reduced reserves in North Hillsboro, and added 1,050 acres (~425 hectares) to the UGB in Northwest Hillsboro while classifying 1,700 acres (~690 hectares) as rural reserves. Despite this, efforts to reclassify the land resurfaced. In 2017, SB 186 proposed converting the 1,700 acres in Northwest Hillsboro from rural to urban reserves to boost land values, but it failed. A similar 2018 attempt, HB 4075, also failed under heavy opposition. By the early 2020s, however, bipartisan consensus around attracting semiconductor investments revived the issue. Political leaders argued that UGB expansion was essential to lure Intel and other firms, along with state subsidies. In 2023, following recommendations from the Semiconductor Task Force and the Joint Committee on Semiconductors, Oregon passed SB 4, the Oregon CHIPS Act. The Act created a semiconductor fund to complement federal CHIPS investments, allocating USD 90 million to Intel, while introducing an R&D tax credit and an Industrial Land Loan Program. Oregon leaders also hoped Hillsboro might host the planned National Semiconductor Technology Center, though the award ultimately went to Sunnyvale, California (the original ‘Silicon Valley’). Section 10 of SB 4 granted the governor temporary authority to bring new land into existing urban growth boundaries for semiconductor and advanced manufacturing uses—up to two sites larger than 500 acres (~200 hectares) and six sites under 500 acres. The statute also allowed Hillsboro to acquire 1,700 acres of farmland if a semiconductor firm or supplier required additional land (Knudsen 2024). In March 2024, Intel announced a USD 36 billion investment in its Hillsboro campus after securing federal CHIPS Act support and USD 115 million from Oregon's program.8 Later that year, residents of North Plains opposed a proposed 855-acre UGB expansion for semiconductor suppliers and petitioned for a referendum. The legislature blocked the effort with HB 4026, backed by the city's mayor, council, and local senator (Rogoway, 2024b). Friends of North Plains Smart Growth pledged to sue if the expansion proceeded. At the same time, a 373-acre parcel north of Hillsboro was identified for possible inclusion under SB 4, and public meetings were held in late 2024. However, Governor Tina Kotek declined to issue the required executive order before the December 31 deadline, leaving no lands converted under SB 4's authority. Intel's financial troubles provided important context for this decision. By the end of 2024, the company reported nearly USD 19 billion in global losses (Intel, 2025). In 2025, under new CEO Lip-Bu Tan, it began laying off about 2,400 workers in Oregon—roughly 12 percent of its local workforce across campuses in Aloha and Hillsboro. At the time of writing, Intel is expected to remain an anchor of Oregon's economy, but with a smaller workforce and a likely shift toward R&D, design, and advanced node development rather than broad fab expansion. Future large-scale projects will still hinge on state and federal incentives, regulatory changes, and whether Oregon can provide suitable land and infrastructure. Advanced-node production would also require far greater energy and water use than earlier generations, demanding major infrastructure upgrades even without new land brought into the UGB. Discussion

In The Dalles, Google bound the city's fiscal and hydrological systems to confidential energy and water contracts, embedding local governance within the firm's private infrastructure logic, a pattern repeated across the US. In Morrow and Umatilla Counties, Amazon's data centers transformed a rural electric cooperative into one of Oregon's largest greenhouse gas emitters, while its mix of gas-fueled power cells, private tariffs, and opaque financing structures deepened local inequalities even under the banner of renewable procurement. Intel's stalled expansion in Hillsboro, meanwhile, illustrates the volatility of anchoring territorial futures to globally mobile capital. Despite extensive state incentives and statutory reforms, its local impact remains limited. Collectively, these cases show how a single industrial paradigm—cloud capital—produces divergent territorial outcomes depending on institutional and ecological conditions, yet converges on a shared logic of subsidy, opacity, and infrastructural dependency. Building from these observations, the discussion uses the conceptual framework of metabolic coupling, rescaled governance, and infrastructural dependency to theorize the emergence of a digital metabolic regime and its socio-ecological effects. First, this emergent regime is defined by metabolic coupling, in which energy, water, and land are increasingly governed as interdependent components of a single infrastructural metabolism sustaining the expansion of cloud capital. Hyperscale operations transform utilities from managing variable peaks to maintaining continuous, contractually guaranteed baseloads, binding public systems to private demand. Each new intertie, substation, or water pipeline binds one system to another, producing interdependencies that are difficult to unwind. Once such couplings are formed, they consolidate into a digital metabolic regime that externalizes ecological costs—emissions, groundwater depletion, and land loss—onto rural and peri-urban territories while benefits accrue to distant data markets. In The Dalles Google's growing demand required new substations, imported power, and an exclusive water entitlement that redirected hydro capacity from community use to server cooling. In Morrow and Umatilla Counties, Amazon's expansion compelled the local cooperative to import fossil energy—with GHG emissions rising from 10,600 tons in 2011 to 1.8 million tons in 2022—and re-engineer effluent systems for reuse. In Washington County, Intel's proposal to extend the urban growth boundary hinged on commitments to redundant power and water capacity, tying land conversion to infrastructural guarantees. Local responses to this reconfiguration of land and resource use have been uneven. Some communities, encouraged by tax revenues and abstract economic development prospects, have embraced further data-center expansion. In Hermiston, for instance, the city council voted to annex nearly 800 acres into the urban growth boundary to attract more facilities, with only one councilor dissenting over the loss of farmland and strain on utilities. Elsewhere, resistance has grown. Cascade Locks rejected a USD 100 million data-center proposal amid concerns over water rights and environmental impacts. In Forest Grove, a similar project was approved despite appeals from residents citing its proximity to homes and potential effects on rates and resources (LaMora, 2025). Across the US, Data Center Watch (2025) reports that between May 2024 and March 2025, over USD 64 billion in data-center projects have been blocked or delayed. Rising resource scarcity has intensified these conflicts. Grid congestion, transmission bottlenecks, and surging construction costs have strained Oregon's capacity to deliver reliable power (Wozniacka, 2025). Utilities such as PGE have added hundreds of megawatts to grid plans, yet delayed projects amid solar supply shortages (Danko, 2023). Transmission siting has also drawn local resistance (Danko, 2024), while the financial burdens remain unevenly distributed. A 2025 Harvard Electricity Law Initiative report found that utilities nationwide are increasingly shifting the costs of powering Big Tech's data centers onto ratepayers through opaque contracts and regulatory loopholes (Martin and Peskoe, 2025). In Oregon, this hidden subsidization prompted the 2025 POWER Act, which requires data centers to pay proportional infrastructure costs and sign decade-long contracts to protect residential and small-business customers. Companion bills, HB 2065 and 2066, authorize ‘microgrid zones’ intended to decentralize energy control, though these could equally become new vehicles for financial speculation and industrial capture if dominated by private energy–finance coalitions. While solutions to energy issues are put forward, water conflicts are even harder to compartmentalize. Between 2019 and 2024, multiple counties declared drought emergencies, with six of the past ten years among the driest on record. A 2024 state report documented declining streamflows, groundwater depletion, and decades of over-allocation without proper assessment of available resources—conditions that amplify uncertainty for planners and utilities alike (Chamberlain, 2024; Oregon Water Resources Department, 2024). In The Dalles, farmers and tribal governments opposed Google's groundwater withdrawals, citing secrecy and risks to senior water rights that sustain regional livelihoods and legal priority (Osaka, 2023). With semiconductor fabs and new hyperscale data centers projected to consume tens of million gallons per day, competition among industrial, municipal, and agricultural users will likely intensify as each sector pursues fixed supplies under rising delivery costs (Heisler, 2023; Figueroa, 2024). Second, these resource transformations drive a rescaling of governance as authority over infrastructure shifts from public deliberation to private contractual and executive modes. Oregon's early 2000s data centers moved through relatively transparent local processes—BPA hydropower, land-use hearings, and city negotiations over zoning, infrastructure, and incentives. Over the past two decades, however, hyperscale demands have relocated decision-making into PPAs and special-service contracts, administrative dockets, and executive instruments designed for speed and certainty rather than accountability. Utilities and state agencies now act as facilitators of digital expansion, with increasingly limited avenues for public challenge once deals are struck. The mechanisms of this rescaling are embedded in PPAs, green tariff programs, and interconnection contracts that tether public infrastructure to private demand. Utilities now structure long-term renewable deals for single corporate customers for ‘sustainability’. Intel's fifteen-year contract with Avangrid for a 138-megawatt solar plant in Wasco County, executed through PGE's Green Future Impact program, exemplifies this dynamic. Such arrangements recast utilities from suppliers into co-investors whose financial plans hinge on a few hyperscale clients. State institutions have adapted accordingly. Oregon's Energy Facility Siting Council expedites large-scale approvals, utilities file specialized interconnection contracts beyond the scrutiny of general rate cases, and city governments negotiate water and wastewater guarantees that bind local systems to future digital expansion. In practice, these instruments convert private build-out ambitions into public obligations through technically dense paperwork that is hard to access and largely insulated from contestation. Federal and regional reforms—largely invisible in the Oregon cases—have scaled up these contractual and executive forms of rule, converting infrastructure development into a domain governed through administrative procedure rather than public debate. Under FAST-41, major projects move onto an executive, timeline-driven track that front-loads interagency coordination and compresses environmental review, shifting substantive decisions from open hearings to coordinated bureaucratic processes. At the same time, FERC has recoded grid access and expansion as tariffed obligation. Order 2023 standardizes interconnection timelines, financial readiness screens, and cost assignments, while Order 1920 mandates long-term regional transmission planning and codified cost sharing. These frameworks turn queue position, deliverability, and network upgrades into legally enforceable entitlements settled through docket filings rather than deliberative public forums. Within this technocratic architecture, hyperscale buyers such as Google and Amazon Energy—as both the largest users9 and independent energy companies themselves—have pushed for an investment-oriented logic of grid reform with uniform timelines, fixed deadlines, and clear cost-allocation rules to synchronize grid access with corporate construction schedules (see, for example, Google, 2022; Amazon Energy, 2023). Meanwhile, the Western Energy Imbalance Market (see Figure 5) and the forthcoming Extended Day-Ahead Market institutionalize cross-state trading and centralized dispatch, embedding Oregon's utilities in regimes where regional market logic increasingly bridges over territorial regulation. While enhancing resilience and providing a speedier buildout, these shifts place decision-making increasingly outside democratic arenas. Substantive authority now resides in long-term contracts, administrative orders, and market platforms optimized for capital mobility, while traditional venues—public hearings, planning commissions, and utility boards—risk becoming procedural formalities. By converting utilities into constant suppliers for energy-intensive operations and binding those commitments across energy, water, and land systems, cloud capital entrenches asymmetric relationships that privilege private flexibility over public capacity. Utilities such as Umatilla Electric and PGE, though institutionally distinct, are now structurally reliant on a handful of hyperscale clients whose loads dominate forecasting, procurement, and investment decisions. These dependencies are actively engineered through financial instruments—PPAs, build-transfer leases, and green bond issuances—that transform utilities into intermediaries for global capital flows. Crucially, these agreements are often signed not by recognizable corporate entities but by shell subsidiaries—Amazon's Vadata or Google's Design LLC—that capture tax incentives and isolate liability. Public records typically list only these intermediaries, legally obscuring who bears ultimate responsibility if projects are delayed, downsized, or abandoned. This opacity masks significant financial and regulatory risk. Throughout 2025, financial commentators have begun to warn of overcapacity in AI infrastructure, noting parallels to earlier cycles of overbuild in energy and telecom sectors (Elder, 2025; Ip, 2025; Lutz and Lichtenberg, 2025) followed by the Bank of England and the International Monetary Fund in October 2025. If cloud demand slows, subsidiaries could default, triggering cascading liabilities. Historical precedents suggest how this might unfold (although present interdependencies are much more complex). In 2018, FirstEnergy Solutions sought to abandon long-term PPAs during bankruptcy, revealing the fragility of supposedly binding contracts. Earlier deregulation waves saw utilities recover billions in stranded costs from ratepayers through surcharges—costs that effectively socialized private risk. When infrastructure financed for expansion becomes underutilized, local budgets shrink, pension funds lose value, and ecological stresses persist as utilities continue operating facilities built for vanished demand.

Dependency, in this sense, is not merely a side effect of digital expansion but a mechanism of power that aligns state institutions with the imperatives of accumulation while foreclosing alternative pathways for public or ecological governance. The

The same contracts that stabilize markets for investors constrain the capacity of states and communities to redirect infrastructure toward public or ecological ends. When downturns reveal hidden obligations, the public inherits systems optimized for private expansion but likely ill-suited for collective resilience. In this light, the Oregon case reads less as an exception and more as an early signal of how these liabilities travel through territory. Conclusion At first glance, Oregon's hydropower, protective land use law, and progressive energy policy positioned it as an ideal test case for sustainable digital growth. Yet even under these favorable conditions, cloud expansion has produced scarcity, opacity, and new dependencies. If one of the best-prepared US states struggles to manage the strain, the implications for less-prepared regions are starker. Utilities are already recalibrating to this demand: investor-owned and public providers plan to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on the grid in 2025 and more than USD 1.1 trillion through 2029 to accommodate rising load from AI/data centers and broader electrification (EEI, 2025). Governments are matching this shift by reshaping energy policy around data-center reliability, in some cases reviving fossil assets and fast-tracking approvals. Georgia has reversed coal-plant closures, Pennsylvania and West Virginia are leaning into natural gas, and the United Kingdom and several US states have created industry-led councils to accelerate permitting for energy and data-center projects for competitiveness and national security. Oregon thus serves not as a leading indicator of a wider reorganization of territorial development around the infrastructural demands of cloud capital. The shifts illustrated in the Oregon cases extend urban political ecology into the domain of digital infrastructure (see Cugurullo et al., 2025) by showing that data centers and fabs inaugurate a new phase of metabolic urbanization in which energy, water, and land are deliberately planned as interoperable service layers for rapid capital accumulation. Whereas classical UPE emphasized how urbanization externalizes environmental costs, the contemporary problem is that infrastructural integration now internalizes corporate priorities within the state itself. In this context, metabolism no longer describes only the circulation of resources sustaining urban life; it also encompasses the infrastructures that provision ‘national computing power’ for geopolitical competition (Kollar and Stokols, 2025).

This study contributes to long-standing debates on privatization and state capacity by showing how governance itself becomes infrastructural—distributed across contracts, tariffs, and delegated authorities rather than centralized decision-making. Addressing these challenges requires rebuilding state capacity to govern coupled infrastructures at the scales where decisions now materialize. Acknowledging the need for variegated pathways of resistance and pressure amidst rising authoritarian politics, three policy directions follow. First, transparency and permitting must be integrated. Approvals for large digital facilities should jointly assess energy, water, and land impacts and tie incentives to verified performance metrics for emissions, withdrawals, and conversion. Second, the binding terms of expansion must return to partial public oversight through mandatory disclosure of load profiles, volumetric use, and cost-allocation frameworks, alongside community-benefit and accountability clauses. Third, risk and cost must be rebalanced by linking tax abatements and grid investments to measurable public returns and protecting small users through proportional capacity payments or standby charges. Where state pre-emption curtails local power, rules must still provide veto or compensation mechanisms for affected tribal and agricultural communities. Ultimately, Oregon's experience underscores that under cloud capitalism, infrastructural politics is less about expanding capacity than deciding whose world's public systems are built to sustain. The decisive choices—how energy is allocated, who bears cost (and risk), and where authority resides—now occur in executive and contractual venues optimized for speed, not deliberation. Re-politicizing the cloud thus demands institutions capable of governing digital metabolic regimes as coupled systems and restoring democratic oversight to decisions currently made in technical and financial backrooms. Only by relocating these choices into arenas of public accountability can technological modernization be reconciled with ecological limits and the collective right to shape the infrastructures on which contemporary life depends.
